chapter: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
title: How the union started and Howard became financial secretary
summary: Howard says the early bands were nonunion, that he had nothing to do with forming Local 767, and that he took his outside experience inside the union.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: (Recording interrupted.)
Paul?
Yeah.

I just have a few more questions about what the union situation was at that time. Was it all nonunion when you started working with your bands, or what happened, for instance, when you really began to get into unions? I know later on you were a big part of forming the union. You were an official or something in Local 767. How did that all come about, can you tell me?
Well, yes. How did that come about?
Yeah, I mean, the union.
The union? Well, --
In the beginning it was probably nonunion, wasn't it, when you first --
Yeah, it was nonunion. But they soon got that straightened out. It didn't take long, because we were always pushing to do the right thing. And that was the right thing, to have a union band.
Was it the white union in -- Local 47, was that existing at the time?
Yes, it was existing, yeah.
Local 47 had already come out here?
Local 47 -- oh, no, no, no.
Oh, there was no union in Los
Angeles.
No, there was no union, no. All this came up after the union. The union came up after all this, that's what I should have said, yeah.
But then, the white union was formed and then you still as a black musician couldn't get into the white union, is that right?
Oh, we could get into it all right, but it took a little time.
Yes.
You couldn't just --
Couldn't just join?
Couldn't just jump up and join.
So what did you have to do, form your own union? Is that what happened, later on?

No, we didn't form our own union. What we did was try hard to take certain pieces out of the band and make it worthwhile, try to sell them a bill of goods. On everything that I tried to do, I tried to be a gentleman, scholar and everything. That's the only way I could figure it out.
But we had all the union men we could keep up together at that time. Keep together.
So, about what year, do you remember when you did form the Local 767? Do you remember when that
Oh, I had nothing to do with forming it.
Do you know who did at the time? Were there any names that you remember?
Local 767?
Yes, who helped form that?
No, I don't.

But then you became involved at what point, do you know, when -- all I remember when I was a young member and just getting in was that you were financial secretary and was more or less running the whole thing. You seemed to be the strong post of the whole union.
Well, I was, then. But I took mine from the outside and put it in the inside. Does that sound like anything to you?
That sounds good, yes. You took all your experience, the same as you had been doing as a musician.
Yes.
Being a leader in developing things.
That's it.

The one point was, did you just decide to run for an office in the union? How did that come about? You know, Here you are, a musician with a for the band, and all of a sudden, you're financial secretary of the black union. You just
decided --
Well, I don't know. I can't -- I have to think of it a little while, Buddy, and then I'll be able to tell you.

Okay. This is interesting, because we'd like to know -- we knew you were an outstanding leader and instrumentalist, and at the same time you were outstanding as a financial secretary and running the union and keeping it together.
If I have a chance to think on it a little while, it'll come to me and then I'll be able to tell you. And I'd rather tell you the truth than tell you a lie.
Yeah, yeah.
That's the truth. You know me better than that. Yeah.
(Laughter)
